stem:
A 10-year-old child has periumbilical pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant with anorexia and fever. Examination shows localised tenderness with guarding.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Abdominal ultrasound before any surgical referral, because imaging is required to confirm appendicitis in children
options.explanation: Appendicitis is a clinical diagnosis. RCH reserves ultrasound for the uncertain case: it is operator-dependent, sensitivity is around 85%, and a non-visualised appendix is common, so a negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis.

options.label: B
options.text: CT abdomen as the mandatory first-line imaging study
options.explanation: CT carries a radiation dose and is not first-line in children; it is considered only when the diagnosis stays unclear after surgical review and ultrasound.

options.label: C
options.text: Colonoscopy to directly visualise the appendiceal orifice
options.explanation: Colonoscopy has no role in suspected appendicitis and is unsafe in an inflamed bowel.

options.label: D
options.text: Surgical review now on the clinical picture; ultrasound only if the diagnosis remains uncertain
options.explanation: Migratory pain, anorexia, fever and localised RIF tenderness with guarding is appendicitis until proven otherwise, and the surgeons decide on the clinical picture. Ultrasound is for the equivocal case, not a gate before referral.

options.label: E
options.text: Discharge with analgesia, since pain that migrates argues against appendicitis
options.explanation: Migration from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa is the classic history FOR appendicitis, not against it.

context:
Appendicitis in children is a clinical diagnosis: migratory pain, anorexia, fever and localised RIF tenderness go to the surgeons, not to the scanner. RCH uses ultrasound only when the picture is uncertain.

Ultrasound is operator-dependent, misses about 15%, and often cannot see the appendix at all; a normal scan therefore does not exclude appendicitis. CT is kept for the persistently unclear case because of the radiation dose.
